clean_methods: Context: To map how surface chemistry shifts frictional instability boundaries, Method: We will conduct mechanical testing using our PDMS mock finger across six different surface coatings and 16 combinations of finger sliding velocity (5, 10, 25, and 45 mm/s) and applied mass (0, 25, 75, and 100 g plus 6 g finger weight).
Context: To test whether humans can discriminate surfaces by instability differences, Method: We will perform three-alternative forced choice tests with 10 participants across 600 total trials.

Context: To infer whether behavioral performance depends on instability differences rather than conventional friction metrics, Method: We will use generalized linear mixed models (GLMM) to correlate participant accuracy and response times with differences in instability frequencies between surface pairs.

Context: To test whether instability-based predictions outperform conventional surface descriptors, Method: We will compare these correlations against traditional metrics including average friction coefficient, surface roughness, and contact angle hysteresis.
Context: To provide controlled stimuli that differ only in surface chemistry, Method: We will construct "minimal" tactile surfaces using vapor deposition of silanes onto silicon wafers.

Context: To generate reproducible mechanical friction traces that approximate human finger mechanics, Method: We will create a PDMS mock finger that mimics human finger mechanical properties, including appropriate stiffness (100 kPa), a rigid "bone" component, and surface treatment to replicate the stratum corneum.

Context: To define the instability categories used in mechanical and human comparisons, Method: We will categorize friction traces into three broad phases based on competition between adhesion and finger elasticity: steady sliding (constant friction force with high-frequency oscillations), slow frictional waves (large oscillations at frequencies lower than microscopic stick-slip), and stiction spikes (singular large-magnitude events preceding smoother traces).

Context: To capture repeated instability events for each surface and condition, Method: We will collect friction force traces at 550 Hz sampling rate, gathering nine traces per mass-velocity combination for each surface to observe multiple instability occurrences.

Context: To choose human test stimuli that span meaningful instability differences, Method: We will select six pairs of surfaces with varying ranges of instability differences based on mechanical testing results.
Context: To operationalize the odd-one-out discrimination task, Method: Participants will be presented with three surfaces (two identical, one different) and asked to identify the odd sample.

Context: To constrain human exploration to the same motion regime as the mock finger, Method: Participants will use only vertical downward motions with their dominant index fingers to mimic mechanical testing conditions.

Context: To confirm that human exploration produces the same instability types identified mechanically, Method: We will conduct a two-alternative forced choice task where participants explore surfaces while we measure tangential and normal forces in real-time, allowing us to identify the same instability types observed in mock finger testing.
